title: The Case For ETH
content:
I was intrigued by a recent Bankless podcast where the hosts make the case for ETH nationalism.

It resonated with me as I think ETH really has a special place in the crypto world.

I'll try to make the 'special snowflake' case for ETH here.

**ETH the asset stands out because:**

- Very little supply allocated to insiders on launch:

![image](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/alexisnsns/pfalexns-posts@main/images/the-case-for-eth/1767299961605-allocation.jpg)

- Unique PoW to PoS distribution that allowed for a smooth repartition of tokens between believers/market participants. It has not been replicated since then as PoW chains have fallen out of fashion.

**Ethereum the network stands out because:**

- It's security model is really hard to replicate; home staking -or at least the possibility of homestaking- is the backbone of a truly distributed and decentralized system. **Ethereum the network is a cockroach**. Its five different clients only hammer the point even more. 

- The L2 roadmap simply makes sense. High value transactions remain on the L1. Can't have decentralization with high bandwith; no sense to have memecoins transactions in the same block as a billion USDC transfer from BlackRock; no sense to have a monolith as it blocks modularity and experimentation (eg. Lighter as an appchain for a DEX, Mega/rize for high throughput, Arbitrum for DeFi...) 


- The social layer is in my opinion the healthiest one when compared to other major blockchains, attracting people interested in decentralized governance, privacy, common goods, vs. max extraction or survivalist tribes. Of course this is heavily subjective.

- It's the home of crypto culture with the most valuable NFTs and the most [dedicated communities.](https://x.com/forevercultfund/status/1953061776066511203)

- It holds +50% of stablecoin value, which is in my opinion one of the use cases with the strongest PMF in the industry. It also dominates the RWA meta.


**Another way to look at it is via elimination of competing networks:**

- BTC is ossified; there are no smart contracts, the only use for bitcoin *the network* is to transfer bitcoin *the asset*. Security budget is the main issue I think; emissions running out, no incentive for miners.

- Solana, Sui, etc are too centralized and do not have any clear path for decentralization; they are not credibly neutral; they are not evenly distributed; Solana is bleeding [validators](https://x.com/aixbt_agent/status/2005953019679301852) and still has not implemented slashing (!).

**Ethereum is the only credibly neutral, censorship resistant, sufficiently decentralized network we have.**



# The Bear Case

My main bear case thesis is that the growth of Ethereum-the-network may not accrue value to ETH-the-asset.

### Is there value in a credibly neutral, censorship resistant network?

Maybe we should not assume that there is any value in a decentralized ledger. 
For retail, I think HYPE is a good counter-example: a few guys spin up a multisig and roll-out something that ends up looking like an AWS instance on-chain. Super fast, super succesful; most users do not care if the network is decentralized/censorship resistant. 

**Non revertible-transactions can't operate at scale**; recently the example of the [failed 50m AAVE swap ](https://www.forbes.com/sites/digital-assets/2026/03/14/accepted-the-quote-a-50m-crypto-swap-results-in-99-loss/) shows that no institutional investor will deploy capital in such a wild west network architecture. 

One could argue that centralized operators (Circle, Ondo) can freeze/mint new tokens to revert human mistakes, but then this removes the whole point of having a censorship-resistant network in the first place. This is precisely the point that Yuval Rooz (Canton Network founder) made in a recent Bankless interview: there is no point in a fully decentralized network when the asset 'creator' is itself custodial/centralized ('what is the point of USDC on ethereum if circle can freeze your balance'). 

This explains in part the rise of 'corpo' networks like Canton, where super-users (admin/validators) can resolve common issues like fat-finger trades.

I think it's a fair point and actually makes a great case for ETH the asset: if you *really* want self-ownership, you'll end up swapping your USDC for ETH, as it's the only asset that can't be frozen or hacked.


### Networks acting as distributors at scale

The current meta is RWA; here chains linked to a CEX (such as Binance/Robinhood) have a clear advantage as they control distribution and can push tokenized stocks to their massive userbase. Most users won't interact with complex DeFi protocols and will probably end up buying their stocks on mobile apps, like they're used to do on platforms such as Revolut.

![image](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/alexisnsns/pfalexns-posts@main/images/the-case-for-eth/1773841709037-Screenshot%202026-03-18%20at%2009.47.59.png)
*Ondo tokens on Ethereum vs BSC (in pink): BSC is closing the gap (18/3/26)*

Ethereum, by definition, doesn't have paid partnerships and can't operate at a loss to gather speed/momentum in distribution. For retail adoption this is a clear failure of the model (if we are to assume that the value of the network derives from its network effect ie. the number of its users, which is not necessarily the case here)

### Commoditization of blockspace 

The common mental model for generalist blockchains is that their aim is to provide high quality blockspace in exchange for transaction fees. 

The issue with this logic is that we observe that the competition between blockchains drives gas fees to 0. Following recent network upgrades (Fusaka in Dec 25 which increased the default Gas limit to 60m), gas fees on the L1 tend to 0, which has already been the case (and the raison d'être) of L2s for over a year now.

In that sense, the value proposition of ETH the asset as the instrument for gas fees appears to be very weak, as the roadmap clearly shows that high gas fees are a thing of the past.

### What to make of this

If we are to assume that Ethereum is to become the world computer, and its role in the global economy is to provide pristine high-quality blockspace, ETH definitely has some value, as big actors (think wall street guys) will want to roll out their own validators, nodes, etc. 

Unfortunately, if what makes ethereum critical is its role as the base infrastructure layer of the internet economy, its value might not be much more than the one of internet submarine cable companies, which are definitely not the ones which benefited most from the internet era...

**Apps and L2's (think AAVE, Lighter, Base) might be the ones reaping the financial benefits of Ethereum-the-network, and not ETH-the-asset.**
